newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Europeans want gene-altered U.S. soybeans identified.
newsitem.headline: Europeans want gene-altered U.S. soybeans identified.

text.p: U.S. soybean farmers risk seeing European consumers shun their 1996 harvest unless they separate gene-modified strains from unmodified ones to allow labelling of the derived products, European food retailers said Thursday.

The warning from EuroCommerce, which represents the retail and wholesale sector in 20 European countries, comes as U.S. farmers prepare to start this year's harvest, which includes the first batches of a genetically altered soybeans developed by St. Louis-based Monsanto Co.

"I think the farmers in the U.S. should be aware that almost 50 percent of their harvest is in danger, their market is in danger and people might have the tendency to look for other products which do not contain soy," EuroCommerce's Heinrich Kroener told a news conference.

He said that while EuroCommerce was not against genetic engineering of food, it wanted its members to have the chance to meet consumers' fears by using labels to show the presence of gene-modified produce in any foodstuffs.
"Our clients should have the choice between genetically modified and unmodified products," he said.

"Forty percent of this harvest will be exported to Europe ... Soy will be used in approximately 60 percent of the foodstuffs which will be sold in our supermarkets in Europe. This is of major importance to us," Kroeger added.
EuroCommerce said that gene-modified strain made up about 2 percent of the United States's 61-million ton soybean crop.

The American Soybean Association said last July in a letter to EuroCommerce that the gene-modified strain had been approved by regulatory bodies in the United States, Europe, Japan, South America and Canada.

"Segregating a soybean which is unidentifiable from another and labelling foods which may go through multiple stages of processing from the farm to the finished product is neither practical nor informative," the Association said in a letter released to reporters by EuroCommerce.
The Association confirmed the letter as genuine and added that labelling would mislead consumers.
"We agree to labelling if it's to provide information. When there's no difference between (soybean derivatives) it's misleading," ASA's Joe Zak told Reuters.
EuroCommerce said that tests were now available to identify modified and unmodified soybeans.
